Equivocate

ih-KWIV-uh-kayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To equivocate is to use unclear, evasive wording intentionally, especially to avoid committing to a position or to mislead.

Rather than admit the product had failed, the CEO equivocated in every interview that week.

Worked Example

The spokesperson equivocated for ten minutes, using so many qualifiers that no one could tell if the merger was actually happening.

Piling on qualifiers until no one can tell what's true is exactly equivocating.

Your Turn

Answer correctly to continue.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

waffle: To waffle is to keep changing your position because you genuinely cannot make up your mind -- band today, soccer tomorrow. To equivocate is different at the root: the speaker has an answer and hides it, choosing cloudy wording on purpose.

hedge: To hedge is to protect yourself when you are unsure or unwilling to over-promise -- adding 'probably' and 'we'll see' so you cannot be pinned down later. To equivocate goes beyond self-protection: it uses that vagueness to leave a listener believing something untrue.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

clarify: make a statement fully clear

Where it sits · how far the words dodge the truth — qualify → equivocate → double-talk

qualify vs. equivocate: To qualify a statement means adding a small limit or condition, an ordinary part of careful speech -- far milder than to equivocate, which means burying the truth under so many qualifiers that nothing clear remains.

double-talk vs. equivocate: Double-talk pushes further than equivocate into intentional nonsense or contradiction, while to equivocate can be quieter -- technically true wording that still avoids a real answer.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — equi-

prefix — equi-: equal (Latin (aequus))

root — voc

root — voc: voice, call (Latin (vox, vocis))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make, to do (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Equivocate combines Latin aequus ('equal') + vox ('voice') -- literally 'of equal voice,' describing words that carry two equally possible meanings at once.

Use the root in a new word: voice

Use the root in a new word: voice: The same vox root gives us the everyday word voice itself -- both words are built on that same root for speaking or being heard.

Root Check

Word Choice

Equivocate focuses on intentionally unclear wording chosen to avoid commitment, distinct from Prevaricate (taught in this same unit), which focuses on the broader act of evading a direct question by any means, not just wording.
